utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Ms. Chittenden, welcome again to the courtroom. The next witness is ready, is it the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in the courtroom. Our next witness is Witness 116, who will be known by the pseudonym PW-049. He will be testifying with facial distortion today, and yes, he is ready to be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the witness will be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation to tell the truth which is shown to you on the card now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please sit down. You know the procedure in this Tribunal. There are protective measures in place for you, and I think Ms. Chittenden, for the Prosecution, has some questions for you. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: We met on Wednesday. My name is Caitlin Chittenden and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could we have P720 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see something come up on the screen now. Please could you read it to yourself and confirm that it's your name written next to PW-049.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Is that your name in front of -- next to PW-049, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this as an exhibit under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall providing a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 26 February 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your statement at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review that statement before coming to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you respond in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to offer into evidence the witness's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. It is P719, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor and Popovic et al. on 6 March 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your testimony at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to listen to that testimony again before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: The same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to offer into evidence the witness' testimony in Popovic. It is P717, under seal; and P718, public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I would also like to offer into evidence at this time the two intercepts admitted as exhibits during that testimony. For the record, they are P723, A and B, and P724, A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's OTP statement and testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, after I read out the summary, I'll have a few further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may move into private session for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: In 1994, the witness joined the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit of the ABiH 2nd Corps and was assigned to the southern site upon the invitation of his platoon commander. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: (redacted). At the southern site, the witness's platoon of ten men worked in shifts of ten days, rotating every 8 hours. The witness described the procedure he used to intercept, record and transcribe radio communications, and this is set out in paragraph 3 of his witness statement, Exhibit P719. Once an intercepted conversation was transcribed, it would be forwarded to the typist who would type, date, and send out reports of the conversations to the command in Tuzla. The witness worked at the southern site until he was demobilised in November 1996. Prior to the witness's testimony in the Popovic case, he reviewed originals and photocopies of two handwritten intercepts which he confirmed he had intercepted, recorded and transcribed. For the record, these are P723 and 724A. The witness also reviewed two typewritten print-outs of intercepts and confirmed that they contained the same conversation as the two intercepts he confirmed transcribing. For the record, these are P723 and 724B. Your Honours, that concludes my summary, I now have a few questions to ask the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a booklet of four intercepts that we have compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please may I ask for the assistance of the Court Usher. For the record, these intercepts are Exhibits P721 through 724.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I don't want to you look in detail through every page in this booklet, but can you please turn to each of the four red tabs I have marked and let me know whether you recognise your handwriting on these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the intercepts the witness is looking at are Exhibits P721 through 724A, and I have just tabbed them so he can navigate easily through the booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, please now could you look through the intercepts that I've tabbed in red on the top and let me know if you recognise your handwriting, and I also have the original notebooks here if you find that easier to look at.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Were you the operator who recorded and transcribed these four intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you review these four intercepts before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you also review the four -- sorry, the original notebooks containing those four intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Do the copies in the booklet there conform to the four intercepts in the original notebooks that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you also review the print-out versions of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And do the print-out versions reflect the same conversations as the handwritten versions of the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd just like to ask you a different question now. In the Popovic case, you were asked about an intercept that you transcribed between Colonel Cerovic and General Krstic at 1132 on 23 July 1995. You testified that you were not sure how you were able to identify Cerovic as one of the speakers as his name did not appear in the text of the conversation. Do you have any additional explanation for that now?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I do. When the conversation was recorded we had devices in front of us that scanned the matter and looked for frequencies, and in front of me, I had an UHER, and the device scans for some time and then stops at the frequency where the voice is heard. And when the colonel, Colonel Cerovic started speaking, I heard it was -- I heard Colonel Cerovic asking to speak to someone else, but I failed to switch the UHER device on straight away, but I did hear his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: For the record, this was P724 in our case, and the reference in the Popovic case to the transcript 6 March 2007, T8332 to 8333, where the witness was asked about this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you about a different topic now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we move into private session for the next couple of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if the intercept operators at the northern site you just mentioned were able to intercept the same conversations as you were at the southern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any specific instances where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Well, yes, in this case I recorded a telegram and I saw that my colleague at the northern site recorded that same telegram.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd like to show you a copy of your telegram or intercept now. If you could turn to the red tab 4 in your booklet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Which is page 723A, for record, behind tab 4 in everyone's intercept booklets. If we could please have this up in e-court, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, if you wouldn't mind opening the intercept booklet and just going to the tab 4. I also have the original if you prefer to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I could ask the Court Usher, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I have a question for the witness. Witness, I just have a clarification, in line 22, page 8 of your -- of the Lotus Notes transcript, to a question you said: "Well, yes, in this case I recorded a telegram and I saw that my colleague at the northern site recorded the same telegram." How did you come to know this, how did you know? Since you were in the northern site and the site where you were at different locations?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreter did not hear the answer. The microphone was not working, thank you. Could the witness repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please go a little bit further towards the microphone, that would be helpful. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second conversation, the one that my colleague recorded, I saw it a few days beforehand and it was almost the same document that I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt you, I will be asking him a few questions about this later which might clarify it. If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, if you can have a look at the original notebook that I just passed to you, which for everyone's records, it's 723A. Can you again just identify that that is your handwriting, please. It's one of the intercepts you looked at this morning.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, let's take a moment to look at this intercept. For the record, we can see on the top of the page the frequency 255.950. We can see the time, which is 1 and then something 58. And the participants. Can you see that? Either on the notebook or on the screen, the participants X, Colonel Deic, and Miletic? Now, Witness, take a moment, as you are doing, to briefly read through the intercepted conversation for us. For the record and for everyone, we can see the conversation goes as follows. On the third line of the conversation, X asks, "Who's there?" D responds, "Colonel Deic." X says, "Is Miletic there?" Then later on, a bit further down in the conversation, X asks, "Has Toso arrived?" M responds, "Yes, he is waiting for you where you told him." X says, "Is there anything to be signed?" M says, "Yes, there's nothing urgent. I mean, there is something, but it's nothing urgent. It can all wait." And X says, "Wait for me at 272." And the conversation finishes a few lines later. Witness, can you see that there that your notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you can just close that notebook for a moment, I'd like to show you a different intercept that we haven't looked at today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I may ask for the assistance of the court usher again. It's behind the green tab in your book, if you'd like to look. And for everyone that's P723C.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'll also pass you this so you can see it more easily. This is the original notebook. Witness, take a look at this intercept here, is this in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, let's take a moment to look at this intercept together. For the record, we can see the frequency 255.950, and I'm halfway down the page in the B/C/S for everyone's information. We can see the time of 1359, and we can see the participants, Colonel Devic, Miletic, and Z. Now, Witness, let's take a moment to briefly read through that conversation together. For the record, we can see the conversation goes as follows. On the first line, which is midway down the page, Z asks, "Who's that?" D responds, "Colonel Devic." Z asks, "Is Miletic there?" Then later on in the conversation, Z asks, "Has Toso come?" M responds, "Yes, he is waiting for you where you told him to wait." Z says, "Is there anything to be signed?" M, "No, nothing that cannot wait." Z says, "Wait for me at 272." Then the conversation finishes a few lines later. Witness, do you recognise the conversation recorded in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, is this an example of a conversation which was intercepted and recorded at both the northern and southern sites?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And, Witness, just to clarify, you were not the operator who recorded this version of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And you became aware and you saw this conversation for the first time when I showed it to you during a proofing session on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And you were not aware of it before that?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: May I ask Your Honours, is that -- does that answer your question or would you like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to wait a moment because the microphone is not working, Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... just to clarify one more thing. In his answer, he said: "The second conversation, the one that my colleague recorded, I saw it a few days beforehand."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may ask him that question again just to clarify, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the Judge's question then. When you responded to Her Honour's question before about when you saw this notebook and this intercept in front of you now and you said "a few days before," what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I saw the telegram, the same telegram -- or, rather, the notes or the same telegram that I recorded and I realised that my colleague recorded the same thing on the west side. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. When did you see this, your colleague's notebook for the first time? When was that?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: A couple of days ago. Two days ago, I don't know. When I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. So just to clarify, it wasn't in 1995 that you were talking about, was it, when you said "a few days before"?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: You were referring to --

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Two days ago when I arrived here, that's when I saw those notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Judge, does that answer your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask an additional question, please. Sir, you are using the term "telegram," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that means a telegram. That means that I heard what I heard, that I recorded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is in your understanding a telegram, what you recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that's the term we used. Telegram. A conversation. We called it a telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like me to clarify that further or is that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you heard Mr. President's question just then. Just so we are clear, when you refer to the word "telegram," are you referring to the conversation that you intercepted, recorded, and transcribed in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's what I've been referring to when I've been questioning you as an intercept or a intercepted conversation. Is that the same thing as a telegram, what you are meaning?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Intercepted conversation, well, yes, but we call them telegrams. That was the habit we had. But, yeah, you can call them intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, is that -- thank you. Your Honours, at this time I would like to admit the intercepts 723C and D into evidence. That is the handwritten notebook of the intercept we've just been looking at with the witness and the printed version, and the printed version should be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that concludes my questions for this witness. However, there is one final document on my exhibit list that I would like to tender and it's P723E, under seal. I won't be asking the witness any questions about this document, and as it is a MUP intercept report which includes verbatim the intercepted conversation we have just seen in P723C and D, and which we have just heard from the witness's testimony was recorded by a colleague of his at the northern site and records the same conversation as his intercept in P723A and B. So I would like to move for this into evidence but I won't be asking the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questioning. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Chittenden. Sir, you know we are now turning to the cross-examination by Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome everybody in the courtroom, the Prosecutor, the witness, yourself. And may peace reign in this house, and may these proceedings finish in accordance with the God's will and not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since you and I speak the same language, we'll have to make breaks between my question and your answer. Every time I finish my question I'll say "thank you" and then you wait for a couple of minutes, two or three minutes, and then you start answering. Thank you. Can we start?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, which is 719 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be displayed on the screen for the benefit of the witness, thank you. We don't have it yet, but yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the first page of your statement that you provided on the 26th of February, 2007. Why didn't you sign this statement in your language and you signed it in English? Is your English better than your own mother tongue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I don't speak English, sir. I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us was the statement typed when you were in being interviewed or was it typed subsequently and then you were subsequently given the statement to sign?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly but it is possible it was typed subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to review the statement before you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to page 2 in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the witness whether he adheres by everything that he said in the statement and whether he agrees that that is indeed the statement that he provided, given the fact that it hasn't been signed?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the second paragraph where it says number 2, line 5, where you say: "I don't know the name of the unit." Did you find it? The

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: (redacted) it says: "I don't know the name of the unit but it was an electronic monitoring unit." Were you able to find that?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Just a moment, bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Line 6, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we have to redact page 17, line 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, it doesn't really matter, just tell us whether you are able to find it in the text?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But can you count in paragraph 2, where it says, "2," we are not going to line 1, we are not going to read line 2, 3, 4, and 5. We are not going to read the first three words in line 6, and then we start reading at -- we are -- "I don't know the name of the unit." Do you see that, "I don't know the name of the unit but it was an electronic monitoring unit"? Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then you read back to me what you read in line 5 in your own language. Line 6.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Line 6: "I don't know the name of the unit but it was an electronic monitoring unit." That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. In the meantime, did you learn the name of the unit from the moment when you provided the statement until today?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what unit that was?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: It was a unit for electronic surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that its establishment name?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: At the beginning there was an abbreviation PEP, P-E-P, and then that was altered into a unit for electronic monitoring and surveillance, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now count from the bottom of the page in the second paragraph, the fifth line from the bottom of the second paragraph, and in that line it says: "We were working in shifts. We were rotating every 8 hours, and one platoon (redacted)"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't really matter. Since you worked in shifts, can you please describe how that happened, how that was organised?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, we did work in shifts and each shift was every hours. There were three of us working in one shift and the others were free. There were three shifts, each lasted for eight hours. That's how things were organised. And we were there for ten days and then after ten days we would go home to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you worked for eight hours in one day, did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Your device, did it have a scanner or an automatic frequency search?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: It did have a scanner. It was not an automatic process, but yes, the frequencies were scanned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also record the date when the conversations were recorded, when transcripts were made?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That was mandatory. And date and the names of the participants in the conversations if we heard their names. If not, then we would just record the names as unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please now look at paragraph 3, line 6 in that paragraph. The first five words we are not going to read, but then it says: "The procedure was such that we noted down the time and the participants. I'm not sure about the date, but I can state that once the conversation was transcribed, it would be forwarded to the typist." And then it says: "In these reports, they put the date of the intercepted conversations." Did you read this?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain, it was not you who record the date, but the typist, was that the case?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Sometimes we forgot to record the date so the typist would correct that and record the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us about the four intercepted conversations that the Prosecution showed you. Did you record the dates or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, I recorded the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will look at the intercepts and we will come to that, but I saw that there was no date either in the handwritten transcript or in the typed transcript.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Sometimes we forgot, but we usually did note the date. Sometimes people forgot to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For example, let's look at P721A. Thank you. Do you see the transcript on the screen, on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you note the date here?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: At the beginning of the telegram, frequency 259.679 [as interpreted], time 1654. Participants Panorama, Mico, and Toso.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see a date here or do you only see the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I don't see a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I see the time but the date is missing. But the commander must have noted the date when he forwarded the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also enclose the tape with the transcript when you forwarded the transcript to the typist?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: After the shift was over the commander took the tapes. He was the one who changed the tapes. And as for the transcript that I recorded, I personally handed it to him and he forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this notebook is some kind of evidence in this trial, how can we establish the date and the credibility of the date based on what you recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Well, most probably there is a date. There must be a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce the second -- the other document that was recorded on the other facility where the -- one of the interlocutors asks, Did Toso arrive?" And the transcript that you recorded, can they be displayed simultaneously, the two transcripts. May we have on e-court the two documents that the Prosecutor showed a moment ago to the witness, where it says that he recorded one at the northern site and the other at the southern site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7231A and 724A. 723A and 724A, but I'm not quite sure of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify for the record. On line -- or page 21, line 12, just I'm not sure -- just to make this clear, the accused stated: "... the Prosecutor showed a moment ago to the witness, where it says that he recorded one at the northern site and the other at the southern site." Just to make sure that's not he recorded both. That's not what the witness's evidence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Chittenden. I apologise if I put it that way. One was recorded in the southern site by the witness and the other on the northern site by his colleague, and you asked them whether they were identical and recorded at the same time so I'd like to show these two parallelly now together. One beside the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are these the right documents now on the screen that you are asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we have the right documents on the screen. They are Prosecution documents which I'm using in this instance, and I'd like to ask the witness to tell us whether there's a date there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, I would only like to clarify if these are really the document you were asking for. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Just a couple of things. First thing, I don't believe they are the documents that Mr. Tolimir is asking for. It should be P723A and C. So that second document I don't believe is correct, the 1132. That doesn't match. Secondly, just to clarify for the record, the accused stated that I asked if the -- line 22, line 2, asked if I asked if they were identical and recorded at the same time. That was not my question. I asked if the conversations were the same, if those recorded the same conversations, not if they were identical and at the same time. So I would just like to clarify that for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have now on the right side of the screen the different document than before. I see on the left side on the top the number 255950 and the same number occurs on the right side in the middle of the page. Are these now the two documents you were asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Those are precisely the two documents that I asked to have called up and I want to ask the witness the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you record these two documents, Witness, that we can see on our screen?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, not both of them, just the first one. I recorded the first one and that is written in my hand; the other one was written by my colleague at the northern site and it's in his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there's a date on the document that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Let me explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just tell me whether there is a date or not and then explain.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, there's not a date, but the date was probably written when it was sent out. And I think I know when this document was sent out. I think I know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at line 15, X is asking, "Has Toso arrived? Is Toso there?" Do you see that? Line 16, "Has Toso arrived?"

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the X is in this transcript? Who is the X and who is the M?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I don't know who the X is. It's an unknown participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you say D, you have a D and X and an M.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Well, probably somebody also -- there was a third person who connected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, who is asking -- who is the X asking, "Has Toso arrived?"

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I don't know. If I knew, I would have written the name and not an X.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So is this some third participant?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, a third participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's not the two people conducting the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, it's probably someone at the exchange, the switchboard that connected the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, look at the right-hand side of the screen and there it says -- well, it's the same conversation. And look at line 11 there.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Z is asking now, "Has Toso arrived?" So there are two participants, Delic and Miletic. Miletic is Z, Delic is D, and then Miletic asks whether I have arrived. So is there a difference in those two documents?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Probably the reception was weaker on my receiver, weaker than my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side, are there three participants or two participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: He has two participants in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise to the interpreters for speeding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can you tell us whether this conversation has a date, when it was recorded? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there's no date but the time is the same. 59 and I have it at 58. So probably our watches weren't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. You were right, Mr. Tolimir, to give an advice to the witness to pause between question and answer, but you don't do that at the moment as well. But you are very fast, you are speaking nearly at the same time but it's very difficult for the interpreters. Please pause before the question and answer. And now carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise once again to the witness for speeding up our communication. Thank you. Can you tell us, to avoid me reading the statement because you said you didn't work with tapes, do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that means and how come you didn't work with tapes? What does that mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Well, it was my job to record the conversations and then to transcribe the conversations on to a piece of paper or a notebook, the intercepted conversation, I mean. And behind me, the commander would be sitting and he had a computer, so I would hand it over to him and then he would forward it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just explain this to us: Did you record the conversations on a tape or on something else?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: On a tape. The UHER, UHER tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you had -- you dealt with tapes until they were handed on?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I recorded the tapes, but I didn't have anything to do with the devices and so the instruments themselves. The commander would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is the following: Do you remember any activities that I performed in the conversation that you recorded and were you able to note that during the proofing days?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Well, the X, unknown participant, and the colleague who put the Z down and recorded it probably had better reception so he could hear more clearly. But according to my document, in my document, I don't know who the X is, I didn't know who X was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now looking at the second document, is it logical that Miletic should ask after me if he is called up by Devic and the only information he wants to obtain is whether Toso has arrived? Is it logical for Miletic to ask Devic where Toso is, whereas Devic is calling up from the field?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I really can't answer that. I didn't write that second conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So in those two documents, is there any word that I uttered, that I spoke, or anything I did?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Not in my document, but in this other one, I don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you just for a clarification related to the document on the right side of the screen. Some minutes ago you identified Z as the speaker Miletic. I would like to ask the witness if that is really Z Miletic. If you look at the left line of this document, you see three different letters, Z, D, and M. Are there three speakers? Perhaps you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness about the left-hand document and he said there were three participants in that conversation, whereas some X is asking whether Toso has arrived, not Devic and Miletic. Whereas on the right-hand side, you have under the frequency and the time 1359, it says Colonel Devic and Miletic and then colon Z. And Delic [as interpreted] says, Colonel Delic [as interpreted]. And then we come to the Z where Miletic asks have I arrived, so he is asking his collocutor who is in the field. So I don't know who is asking after me, since I'm not speaking at all. And this document does not testify to any of my activities, any activity or speech on my part, whereas that's what the Prosecutor announced during his examination of this witness. So I apologise to the witness for having to ask him that. He just helped us to clarify the dilemma that occurs here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I understand that very well, but I was referring to a different problem. On the left column, you see Z, D, Z, D, Z, D, Z, M, Z, M, Z, M, Z, M. I formed the impression that there are three speakers recorded in this transcript, that could be that Z is not Miletic but a third person. Witness, could you say something about that? Have you any knowledge? I know this is not your transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left is the witness's transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm only referring to the right document and I would like to know if the witness can say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that the document was written -- well, the words are the same, but this Z, D, the participants, my colleague probably recorded it better because he had better reception. He could hear the conversation better. That's all I can say about the document. I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for helping us clarify this matter. Ms. Chittenden wanted to say something, she was on her feet, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. I was just going to say, Your Honours, I will clarify this in re-examination, if you like. I can go through with the witness in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, would you recognise my voice if you heard it on a tape in the conversations shown here provided for your testimony in the trial against me?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there any trace in your unit's archive of my voice? Do you know about that? Is there a recording of my voice?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I don't know, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I apologise once again to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have another question. Did you ask for protective measures from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or from this Tribunal? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have your statement back up on the screen, please, which is P71B [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we turn to page 2, paragraph 3, please. We are looking at the page I'm interested in and paragraph 3 there that I'd like to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The third line from the bottom reads as follows: "If there was an interesting conversation, we would switch on the UHER and tape -- start recording this conversation on the tape. Once the conversation was recorded on to the tape, we would listen to it again and write it down on a sheet of paper, or sometimes into notebooks as well, but most of the time on to sheets of paper." Thank you. Can you see that part?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So there's no mention there of any notebooks. Did you have notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: There were notebooks and when I say "paper," I mean notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. In the notebook, did you write it down directly, because you say it's all paper as far as you are concerned, or did you have a sheet of paper and then write it down in a notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: No, we would write it directly into notebooks, on the paper of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did you cross out any possible mistakes or did you delete them in some other way?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: I didn't do that. I didn't cross them out. What was written down was most probably forwarded further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for your sincere answers. Thank you for coming here to talk to me. I wish you a safe journey back home. God bless you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, my cross-examination of this witness is now over, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a first issue, during my direct examination, I inadvertently omitted to move into evidence 721A and B, and 722A and B. They were on my exhibit list and they are two of the handwritten and typed intercepts that the witness identified as his in the booklet. So I apologise, I forgot to request those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to now, Witness, ask you about two things using the notebooks and then my questions will be finished. So first off, I would like to ask about 721A.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we could have that in e-court, please. I apologise, I'd like to show the witness the original notebook and I believe the original notebook in its entirety is P440. So if we could have P440 in e-court, that would be ... Thank you. So this is the original notebook and we'll just -- thank you. And it's page 29 in e-court, if we can ... And that is the same as our Exhibit P721A, that the witness has identified as his, but I'd like to have the whole notebook, please. Thank you, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to pass you the original notebook, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I might have the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And it's also on the screen in front of you, so you can have a look at either the screen or the notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which tape is it in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's 721, so it should be behind the first tab in the binder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Just the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So, Witness, on the left you can see that's the intercept at 1654 hours that Mr. Tolimir was asking you about and that you identified as your handwriting; is that correct? Sorry, Witness, that's one of your intercepts that you've identified as your handwriting? On the left page there.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, Mr. Tolimir, during his cross-examination, asked you to read the top of the intercept and you read that and found there was no date. That's correct, isn't it? Can you just have another look at look at 259.675, which is the frequency. Can you see that there? And then 1654 hours is the time. Then we can see the participants, Panorama, Mico, and Toso. Is that correct, can you see that there?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what I'd like you to do is just turn back a couple of pages in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And if we can also do the same in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to, Witness, look very carefully and see if you can see a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So it should be page 25 in e-court, if we can just go to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, if you can just look very carefully and see if you can see a date on the top of any of those pages, or you can look at the screen, if you like. On the top of that, can you see any date on there?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the date 11 July 19, the rest is not legible. Not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Can you have another look, sorry, can you read out what you can see? What is the first number? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: 17 July.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- okay. If we can -- can you find that in the original notebook, or if it's easier, I can show you the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, may I turn to that page for him in the original. It doesn't matter, it's on the screen, so that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He should try to find it in the original notebook. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, have a careful look, take your time and just see if you can find that page there in the notebook. I think I may have asked you to turn back a bit too far, so we should turn -- turn forward, I apologise. That's correct. Yeah, just look if you can see that page that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Just a moment, bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Just turn back a couple of pages from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it would be helpful if I can direct him just back to the original intercept then he can do it from there because it's, I think, a 60-page book and it might take a bit of time. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I may just ask the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I'll just help you to find it, I know it's a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, could you give the original notebook -- did you find it? If not, you could give it back to Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I'm turning him to his intercept again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Are there any other dates between where you can see the 17 July and where you can see your intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-049
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Bear with me.
